stem: A reviewer argues: "The capability and generality axes are blind to time horizon. A system can look broadly expert-level on them while failing every project that takes several days, so horizon needs its own separate scale." Which response does the framework support best?

options.text: A short horizon shows up as low scores on long-term memory storage and retrieval, which lowers measured generality
A short horizon shows up as low scores on reasoning and mathematics, the domains that long projects stress most
options.provenance: files the horizon limit under the wrong domains; 'Systems scoring poorly on memory naturally fail on multi-day projects' locates it in memory, not reasoning or maths

options.text: Horizon is a deployment property like autonomy, so neither framework should count it toward whether a system is AGI
options.provenance: misreads 'Our working definition does not include the autonomy with which an AGI system operates' as covering time horizon, conflating a capability limit with a deployment choice

options.text: The t in (t,n) tracks response speed, which the CHC speed domain scores, so the two axes cover it already
options.provenance: misreads 'Given a time frame t' as the AI's latency and maps it onto the Speed domain, instead of the time budget for a task

explanation: The reviewer is right that horizon matters but wrong that the axes miss it. Time horizon limitations are implicitly captured in the generality measure as weakness in specific domains, chiefly long-term memory storage and retrieval: a system that cannot retain and recall context fails multi-day projects and scores poorly on those domains. So the two frameworks describe the same deficit from different angles. If you picked reasoning and mathematics, you placed the weakness in the domain that feels hardest, but multi-day failure comes from losing context, not from failing individual inferences. Horizon is also not like autonomy: autonomy is a choice about how a system is deployed, while a short horizon is something the system cannot do. (Defining and Measuring AGI → Defining General Intelligence)
takeaway: Short task horizons are not invisible to the two axes; they appear as low scores in the memory domains.

self_check.cover_test: Yes: a reader who understood the link between the frameworks would say horizon limits surface as weak long-term memory scores inside generality.
self_check.cynic_test: Key and top distractor share an identical frame and differ only in the domain named, so test-taking instinct cannot separate them; the reasoning/maths option is the tempting guess because long projects feel like hard thinking.

stem: A launch post claims System A is "more general than System B, because A handles all ten cognitive domains while B handles only four." On testing, A reaches expert level on two domains; B reaches expert level on all four it handles. Which assessment of the claim is best supported?

options.text: Generality counts only domains reached at expert level, so B is the more general system despite attempting fewer
Generality is an average across the ten domains, so both systems' mean percentiles must be compared before judging
options.provenance: misreads 'outperform 85% of humans in 30% of cognitive domains' as one averaged score rather than two separate numbers, one per axis

options.text: B's expert-level depth on four domains raises its capability, but A's wider coverage still gives it greater generality
options.provenance: misreads 'one model handling writing, math, coding, and visual understanding represents unprecedented breadth' as breadth-of-coverage, missing that a domain only counts at expert-level capability

options.text: Neither system has meaningful generality yet: both fall well short of the AGI threshold on most of the ten domains
options.provenance: misreads the AGI threshold definition as a precondition for having any generality, against 'AGI exists on a continuous spectrum' and early systems being 'genuine general intelligence - just early-stage'

explanation: Generality is the share of cognitive domains where a system reaches expert level. A counts on two of ten (20%); B counts on four (40%), so B is more general even though A attempts more. The launch post measures how many domains a system can produce output in, which is coverage, not generality. If you picked the capability-versus-coverage option, you split depth and breadth correctly but mislabelled breadth: domains a system handles below expert level add nothing to its generality. Generality is also not an average of percentiles, since that would blur the two axes into one number. And a system short of the AGI threshold still has a generality score; the thresholds are overlays on a continuum. (Defining and Measuring AGI → Defining General Intelligence)
takeaway: Breadth counts only where a system is expert; attempting a domain badly adds nothing to generality.

self_check.cover_test: Yes: a reader who knows generality is the percentage of domains at expert level would compute 2/10 vs 4/10 and conclude B is more general.
self_check.cynic_test: A skipper would likely pick the capability-versus-coverage option because it sounds balanced and uses both axes, but it counts attempted domains as breadth; 'expert' appears in two options and all four share length and register.

stem: A news headline asks: "Has AI finally crossed the line into AGI?" Judged by the capability-and-generality framework, what is the main problem with the question itself?

options.text: It assumes a single moment of arrival, when systems improve by degrees on two axes and the label covers a region
It asks too early: nothing counts as general intelligence until it reaches expert level on most domains
options.provenance: misreads the AGI threshold definition ('expert-level performance ... across most cognitive domains') as the entry condition for any generality, against the Wright-brothers passage that early systems 'represent genuine general intelligence - just early-stage (weak AGI)'

options.text: It asks about a real line that cannot be located yet, because benchmarks are too coarse to pinpoint it
options.provenance: misreads 'There's no universally agreed upon threshold' as 'the threshold exists but has not been measured', keeping the binary prior and blaming measurement precision rather than the framing

options.text: It tracks the wrong axis: the line that matters is crossed when systems start acting without human oversight
options.provenance: carries in the charter wording 'highly autonomous systems' from Case Studies and treats autonomy as the AGI line, against 'Our working definition does not include the autonomy with which an AGI system operates'

explanation: The headline treats AGI as an event: one day the system is not AGI, the next it is. We describe systems instead by where they sit on two continuous axes, capability (how good on each task) and generality (on how many domains it reaches expert level), and there is no agreed point where "not AGI" flips to "AGI". The tempting reply that the line is real but not yet located keeps the binary picture and only blames the benchmarks; the problem is the picture, not the measurement. Nor must a system clear expert level on most domains before it counts as general at all: like the Wright brothers' plane, an early general system is genuine but immature, which is what "weak AGI" means. (Defining and Measuring AGI → Defining General Intelligence)
takeaway: AGI names a region of a continuous two-axis space, so "has it crossed the line?" is the wrong question.

self_check.cover_test: Yes: a reader who absorbed the continuum framing would say unprompted that the headline presumes a binary crossing point that the framework denies exists.
self_check.cynic_test: A skipper might pick the measurement-precision option as the most sophisticated-sounding caveat, but it concedes the binary line the key rejects; the key is not the only option naming two axes or degrees in a way that marks it, and no absolutes appear.

stem: The framework insists that AGI sits on a continuum, yet it also offers rough percentile cut-offs for AGI, TAI and ASI. What do those cut-offs contribute that the continuum on its own does not?

options.text: They give safety planning and regulation points at which to act, because risk differs across regions of the space
They reinstate the yes-or-no framing for public audiences, a concession that sits in tension with the continuum
options.provenance: misreads thresholds offered 'When pressed for concrete thresholds' as a retreat from 'AGI exists on a continuous spectrum', missing 'we can't ignore this reality even if generality is a continuous variable'

options.text: They mark where measured risk begins, which is where the continuum turns out to have natural break points
options.provenance: misreads 'here's our interpretation of roughly how terms map onto the (performance, generality) space' as an empirical finding that the space has natural discontinuities

options.text: They let evaluators announce when a system has arrived at each named level, which a smooth scale cannot do
options.provenance: misfiles the purpose of thresholds as declaring arrival, against the stated aim to 'identify thresholds for regulation, and emerging risks before they materialize'

explanation: The cut-offs are overlays for action. A system strong on half the cognitive domains poses different risks from one strong on nine-tenths, and regulation and safety planning need points at which a response is triggered, so we mark rough regions without claiming the space breaks there. That is why they are not a contradiction: the underlying variable stays continuous, and the thresholds are an interpretation laid over it on request, not a return to yes-or-no. They are also not measured facts. We present them as our rough mapping of terms, and other researchers could set them differently. And their job is not to announce that a system has "arrived", which is exactly the semantic debate the continuum was built to avoid. (Defining and Measuring AGI → Defining General Intelligence)
takeaway: Thresholds are stipulated trigger points for safety and regulation laid over a continuum, not natural break points in it.

self_check.cover_test: Yes: a reader who followed the section would answer that thresholds give safety planning and regulation something to trigger on, without conceding that the continuum is broken.
self_check.cynic_test: The 'tension' option is the tempting cynical pick; it fails because the text keeps the variable continuous. 'Continuum' appears in two distractors and 'risk' in the key and one distractor, so no word match picks out the key.

stem: Imagine a system that, on nearly every non-embodied cognitive domain, outperforms most trained professionals but never the very best human. How does the working definition classify it?

options.text: As AGI, because expert-level performance across most domains is exactly the profile the term describes
Short of AGI, because it has only matched strong humans in most domains rather than exceeded them all
options.provenance: conflates the AGI definition ('expert-level performance (80-90th percentile)') with the ASI definition ('superhuman capability (>100%, greatly exceeding all humans)')

options.text: Undecided, because AGI turns on outperforming humans at most economically valuable work, not on domain scores
options.provenance: adopts the quoted OpenAI charter wording as the working definition, missing that such definitions 'lack precision for tracking progress and identifying risks'

options.text: Undecided, because generality turns on how efficiently it acquires new skills, not on its fixed-task scores
options.provenance: files the adaptability view (Chollet, Wang) as the working definition, against 'We acknowledge and incorporate the adaptability focused view's point about efficient learning but prioritize final capabilities'

explanation: Our working definition is a cognitive profile. AGI means matching a well-educated adult's versatility: expert-level performance, better than most people but short of the best, across most cognitive domains. This system fits that profile. The top distractor sets the bar at beating everyone, which is the definition of superintelligence (ASI), not AGI. AGI is expert parity, and ASI is greatly exceeding all humans across virtually all domains. The charter-style test, outperforming humans at most economically valuable work, points in the right direction but is too vague to settle a case like this. The adaptability view is one we acknowledge, but we rank systems on final capabilities rather than on learning efficiency. (Defining and Measuring AGI → Defining General Intelligence)
takeaway: AGI in this framework is expert parity across most domains; exceeding all humans is the ASI definition.

self_check.cover_test: Yes: given the profile, a reader who knows AGI means expert-level across most domains would say 'AGI', and would not demand superhuman performance.
self_check.cynic_test: A skipper might pick 'short of AGI', reasoning that 'general intelligence' should mean beating humans. That is the ASI conflation the item targets. Two options open with 'Undecided', so there is no grammar or register outlier, and the stem gives the profile in qualitative bands rather than recalled percentile digits.

stem: A system performs beyond nearly every human expert at automated ML research and the closely related coding work, and falls well short of expert level at everything else. How do the AGI and TAI definitions classify it?

options.text: TAI but not AGI: TAI can be reached through extreme depth in a few critical areas, while AGI needs expert level across most
Neither: transformative impact is a later stage than AGI, so it cannot arrive before broad expert-level performance does
options.provenance: misreads TAI as a point further along the same scale as AGI, missing the OR-clause 'exceptional capability (99th percentile) on critical domains like automated ML R&D (20% of domains)'

options.text: AGI but not TAI: its superhuman depth counts as general intelligence, while transformation needs reach across the economy
options.provenance: hybrid: reads superhuman single-area capability as generality (against 'Everything along this line ... counts as ANI') and reverses the TAI disjunction into 'low generality cannot be transformative'

options.text: Both: AGI and TAI name the same threshold, one described by cognitive profile and the other by its economic effect
options.provenance: misreads the adjacent AGI and TAI definition boxes as synonyms, missing 'TAI is defined by impact potential rather than cognitive architecture'

explanation: TAI is defined by impact potential rather than cognitive profile, and one of the ways we say it can be reached is exceptional depth on a small set of critical domains such as automated ML research. This system fits that route. AGI is a cognitive-profile definition: expert-level performance across most domains, which this system lacks. The most tempting wrong answer treats TAI as a later rung on the AGI ladder, so impact would have to wait for breadth. That is the ordering many readers bring with them, and the TAI definition deliberately breaks it: a narrow-but-deep system aimed at the right domain could transform the economy while still being ANI on most of the map. Nor are the two terms synonyms. They measure different things and can come apart, as they do here. (Defining and Measuring AGI → Defining General Intelligence)
takeaway: AGI is about breadth of expert-level cognition; TAI is about impact, and extreme depth in the right domain can be enough for it.

self_check.cover_test: Yes: a reader who knows TAI is impact-defined with a deep-but-narrow OR-clause, and AGI needs breadth, would say 'TAI, not AGI' unprompted.
self_check.cynic_test: A skipper might pick 'Neither' on the prior that TAI is the bigger milestone, or 'Both' on the idea that superhuman means advanced; each option names a distinct classification in the same format, and the percentile digits are left out of the stem so recalled numbers cannot decide it.

stem: Two teams deploy the same model weights. One uses it to draft suggestions that a person accepts or rejects; the other lets it carry out multi-step tasks and decide for itself when to check in. What differs between the two setups?

options.text: Their risk exposure: capability is identical, but the agent setup leaves more consequential actions without human review
Their capability level: autonomy is a further step up the same scale, so the agent setup is the more advanced system
options.provenance: misreads 'Just like we had continuous curves for capability and generality, we can similarly have an increasing level of autonomy' as autonomy being a continuation of the capability curve, against 'not what they can do'

options.text: Their inherent danger: holding the model to suggestions shrinks what it is able to do, so the tool setup is a safer system
options.provenance: misreads 'A capable system deployed as a tool (Level 1) might be safer' as a change in the system itself, against 'affects risk exposure, not inherent danger' and 'the underlying capability is identical'

options.text: Their AGI status: general intelligence is defined as autonomous operation, so only the agent setup could qualify as AGI
options.provenance: carries in the quoted charter wording 'highly autonomous systems', against 'Our working definition does not include the autonomy with which an AGI system operates'

explanation: Autonomy describes how a system interacts with humans, not what it can do. The weights are the same, so capability and generality are the same. What changes is how many consequential actions happen before a human sees them, which is risk exposure. The closest wrong answer says the suggestion-only setup is inherently less dangerous. Restricting autonomy does not remove any ability from the model. It changes how much of that ability reaches the world unchecked, which is why we say autonomy affects exposure rather than inherent danger. Treating the agent as the more capable system confuses the two axes. Capability is needed before higher autonomy is possible, but switching autonomy on adds no capability. And our working definition of AGI deliberately leaves autonomy out, even though some lab definitions include it. (Defining and Measuring AGI → Defining General Intelligence)
takeaway: Autonomy is a deployment choice layered on a fixed capability: it changes exposure, not what the system can do.

self_check.cover_test: Yes: a reader holding 'same capability, different deployment' would answer 'how much risk reaches the world, not what it can do' before seeing options.
self_check.cynic_test: A skipper would lean to 'inherent danger' because common sense says tools are safer; that option shares the safety direction with the key, so the choice turns on exposure versus inherent danger, which only the section supplies. No level names or numbers appear.

stem: Two systems end up equally good at writing convincing, targeted phishing messages. System A got there from a handful of examples; System B needed billions of examples and largely memorised patterns. For safety planning, how should they be compared?

options.text: Equal risk from that ability; B's costly route may make it less impressive as an intelligence, not less dangerous
Less risk from B; an ability bought with data and compute rather than learned efficiently is not genuine intelligence
options.provenance: misreads the adaptability view's 'might be less impressive even if both reach the same final capability' as 'less dangerous', against 'the risks exist either way'

options.text: More risk from A; efficient skill acquisition is what general intelligence is, and general intelligence is what drives danger
options.provenance: conflates the adaptability definition ('the efficiency of acquiring new skills') with the safety-relevant quantity, against 'Did it learn efficiently or through brute force? ... These questions don't change the risk profile'

options.text: Equal risk from both; learning efficiency has turned out to say nothing about how intelligent a system really is
options.provenance: misreads 'does the learning path matter more than the destination?' as rejecting the adaptability view, against 'We acknowledge and incorporate the adaptability focused view's point about efficient learning but prioritize final capabilities'

explanation: For safety, what a system can observably do matters more than how it got there. Both systems can produce the same harmful output, so the risk from that ability is the same. This does not mean the adaptability view is wrong, which is where the second 'equal risk' option goes astray. We accept that learning efficiently from few examples says something real about intelligence, and B may well be the less impressive system. We simply rank final capability higher for safety. The option that rates B as less risky makes the common move from 'less impressive' to 'less dangerous'. A phishing message works the same way whether the skill behind it was learned elegantly or memorised by brute force. (Defining and Measuring AGI → Case Studies)
takeaway: Learning efficiency can bear on how intelligent a system is without bearing on how dangerous its abilities are.

self_check.cover_test: Yes: a reader who absorbed 'the risks exist either way' plus 'acknowledge but prioritise final capabilities' would say 'same risk, though B is less impressive'.
self_check.cynic_test: A skipper might spot that two options say 'equal risk' and guess between them, but the choice then depends on whether the adaptability view is rejected or merely deprioritised, which only the section settles; the one absolute ('nothing') sits on a position people genuinely assert.

stem: Two systems end up equally good at writing working exploits for a programming language released after both were trained. System A got there from a few dozen worked examples; System B needed millions of examples and far more compute. The lab argues: "B is less intelligent than A, since it bought its skill with data rather than learning efficiently, so B can ship with lighter safeguards." What is the best assessment of this argument?

options.text: Its premise is defensible, but equal skill at the task means equal risk from it, however the skill was gained
Its premise is mistaken, since a skill counts equally as intelligence however the system came to acquire it
options.provenance: misreads 'does the learning path matter more than the destination?' and the priority on final capabilities as a rejection of the adaptability view, against 'We acknowledge and incorporate the adaptability focused view's point about efficient learning'

options.text: Its conclusion holds, since skill gained by brute-force memorisation tends to break on real-world cases
options.provenance: misreads 'might be less impressive even if both reach the same final capability' as 'less dangerous', against 'whether through efficient learning or brute-force memorization, the risks exist either way'

options.text: Its conclusion holds, since B matches patterns in code without understanding what its output actually does
options.provenance: files the Chinese Room / 'true understanding' objection under the adaptability view, whose objection is about data efficiency; and misses 'Is it conscious or just pattern-matching? These questions don't change the risk profile'

explanation: We accept the lab's premise: on the adaptability view, intelligence is how efficiently a system turns experience into new skills, so a system that needs millions of examples where another needs a few dozen is less impressive even at the same final level. But for safety we prioritise final capabilities, because risk does not depend on the path. Two systems that write working exploits equally well pose the same risk from that skill. The answer that rejects the premise outright mistakes that prioritisation for dismissal of the adaptability view. The memorisation answer is the tempting prior that "bought" skill is fragile and therefore safer, but the case stipulates equal performance, and if a system can do the dangerous task the risk exists either way. Whether B truly understands its output belongs to the consciousness debate, not the adaptability one, and it does not change the risk either. (Defining and Measuring AGI → Case Studies)
takeaway: Learning efficiency can tell you how intelligent a system is without telling you how dangerous its capabilities are.

self_check.cover_test: Yes: a reader who understood the section can say unaided that the adaptability view grants A more intelligence but equal capability means equal risk, so the premise stands and the conclusion fails.
self_check.cynic_test: A skipper might go for the most balanced-sounding 'premise yes, conclusion no' option, so the verdicts are split two 'conclusion holds' and two 'conclusion fails', every option carries a reason clause, the lengths are near-equal (roughly 102-108 chars), and stem words (examples, exploits, learning) were kept out of single options.
